references.text: Isaiah prophesies about 'the son of David' – the Messiah who will sit on David's throne. The blind man's cry, 'Jesus, you son of David,' is a messianic confession linked to this prophecy ([ref:Jes 9:6-7|Isaiah 9:6-7]).
Jeremiah prophesies about a righteous branch that will arise from David's line. The cry 'son of David' reflects the expectation of this messianic descendant ([ref:Jer 23:5-6|Jeremiah 23:5-6]).
The psalmist's prayer, 'Be merciful to me, O God' (ἐλέησόν με in the LXX), mirrors the same urgent plea for mercy that the blind man cries out to Jesus ([ref:Sal 51:3|Psalms 51:3]).
Two blind men cry out to Jesus with the same words: 'You son of David, have mercy on us!' – a close parallel passage to the blind man at Jericho ([ref:Matt 9:27|Matthew 9:27]).
The Canaanite woman cries out to Jesus: 'Lord, you son of David, have mercy on me!' – the same messianic title and the same plea for mercy ([ref:Matt 15:22|Matthew 15:22]).
Matthew's parallel account of the blind men at Jericho crying out, 'Lord, you son of David, have mercy on us!' ([ref:Matt 20:30-31|Matthew 20:30-31]).
Mark's parallel account of Bartimaeus crying out: 'Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!' – a direct parallel to Luke's text ([ref:Mark 10:47-48|Mark 10:47-48]).
Matthew opens his gospel by calling Jesus 'son of David,' thereby confirming the messianic lineage that the blind man confesses ([ref:Matt 1:1|Matthew 1:1]).
Paul confesses that Jesus Christ, 'according to the flesh, is descended from David's line' – the theological background behind the cry 'son of David' ([ref:Rom 1:3-4|Romans 1:3-4]).
